Sage-and-Onion Breakfast Sausages

British · Medium · Makes 10 sausages

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The homemade Lincolnshire's softer-spoken sibling: the same coarse-chopped pork base, with sweet cooked onion folded through the mix and the sage doubled. The onion changes everything about the sausage's character — it mellows the pepper, sweetens the fat as it renders, and gives the cooked link a juicy, yielding interior that the all-meat version trades for snap. This is the Sunday-supper sausage as much as the breakfast one, and it is the mixture that medieval English cooks would recognise without a word of explanation. The one technique worth learning here is the onion's preparation: grated and wrung dry, or finely diced and sweated cool — never raw and wet, which weeps water into the mix and loosens the bind. Two routes are given; both work; the grated-wrung route is the old one and the better one.

- **The onion's water is the recipe's one hazard.** A grated onion yields 30–40 ml of juice; wrung hard in a tea towel, it yields half that — and the wrung onion goes in damp-dry, flavour intact, structure safe. Raw-and-wet onion makes a loose mixture that stuffs sloppy and cooks crumbly. - The same cold discipline as the Lincolnshire base: meat and bowl partially frozen, hands cold, the whole mix assembled in under 15 minutes. - Casings soaked 30 minutes and flushed, as ever. Or go skinless — this mixture's softness suits it particularly.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Onion: wrung damp-dry (or sweated and cooled), no wet pockets in the mix.
  • Seasoning: sage doubled, test patty tasted hot and cool.
  • Stuffing: plump even links, pricked, alternately twisted.
  • Rest and cook: overnight dry, medium-low to clear juices, juicy flecked interior.

Sage-and-Onion Breakfast Sausages

Prep: 30 minutes, plus overnight rest · Cook: 20 minutes · Total: Overnight plus 1 hour · Makes 10 sausages

Ingredients

The meat

  • 700 g pork shoulder, cut into 2 cm chunks, partially frozen
  • 200 g pork belly or fatty pork, cut into 2 cm chunks, partially frozen

The onion

  • 200 g onion (2 medium), grated on the fine holes, then wrung hard in a tea towel — or 200 g onion, very finely diced and sweated in 10 g butter until translucent, cooled

The seasoning

  • 8 g fine sea salt
  • 2 g black pepper
  • 12 g dried sage, rubbed fine (or 25 g fresh sage, very finely chopped) — doubled from the Lincolnshire base
  • 1 g ground ginger
  • 1 g ground nutmeg

The binder

  • 60 g rusk or fine dry breadcrumbs
  • 60 ml cold water (less than the plain base — the onion brings its own moisture back)

The casings

  • 1 length natural hog casing (about 2 metres), soaked and flushed — or skinless, shaped in cling film

Instructions

  1. **Chop the meat coarse, as the base.** Pulse the chilled pork to distinct 3–4 mm flecks in two batches; combine in the chilled bowl. Checkpoint — coarse gravel, not porridge — the same standard as the Lincolnshire master, and the same freeze-pulse-rescue if it smears.
  2. **Fold in the onion and seasoning.** Add the wrung onion to the meat, then the salt, pepper, sage, ginger, and nutmeg. Toss through, sprinkle the rusk evenly, add the cold water gradually, and work with your hand 1–2 minutes until sticky and cohesive. Fry the test patty: 1 spoonful, 3 minutes in a pan, tasted hot and cool. Checkpoint — the mix is sticky and holds when squeezed, the onion flecks are distributed throughout with no wet pockets, and the test patty reads sage-forward, onion-sweet, properly salted — a shade bold, because cooking mutes it.
  3. **Stuff and link.** Onto the soaked, flushed casing; feed steadily, let the filling fill, twist 12–15 cm links with alternating twists, and prick each link twice. Checkpoint — plump, even links with slight give under finger-pressure; no wet, loose sections where the onion pooled. Any section that feels underfilled gets gently massaged toward the next twist.
  4. **Overnight rest, then cook.** Refrigerate uncovered 12–24 hours — the rest does double duty here, marrying the seasoning and drying the onion-damp surface. Cook over medium-low in a dry or barely-oiled pan, 12–15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes. Checkpoint — deep, even browning; taut skins; clear juices at a nick; the interior juicy with visible onion flecks and meat grain — softer than the plain Lincolnshire, sweeter, and just as sage-true.

Finish & Plate

In the full English, beside the fried egg whose yolk the onion's sweetness answers; in the sausage sandwich, where it is arguably at its best; at supper, with mash and the pan's oniony juices as the gravy. It also freezes beautifully cooked, and the raw mix (uncased) is the year's best stuffing for a Sunday bird.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Loose, crumbly mix that won't bindWet onion, or too little workingWring the onion hard; the full 1–2 minutes of hand-working
Onion burnt flecks in the cooked sausageRaw onion bits catching against the panGrate finer, or the sweated route
Sausages burstOverfilled or unpricked, as everFinger-pressure give and two pin-pricks
Sage reads barelyUndoubled herb, or old dried sageFresh dried sage (it fades in the jar) and the full doubling

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Storage:** identical to the Lincolnshire base — 3 days raw, 3 months frozen, 3 days cooked. The onion shortens raw keeping by a day at most. - **Variation — apple and sage:** 100 g of the caramelised apple master's apple, finely diced and wrung, replaces half the onion — the Sunday-morning luxury link. - **Variation — the stuffing bridge:** this exact mixture, baked loose in a dish at 180 °C for 35 minutes, is the classic sage-and-onion stuffing — one recipe, two traditions. - **The pair:** make both this and the plain Lincolnshire in one session (they share every step until the onion), fry one of each, and let the household vote — the sausage wars start at home.

Balance is relational, not absolute — a sentence that upgrades every seasoned dish on the site.

The pan-side signals stay the same: taut skin, clear juices, and a give under the tongs that says juicy rather than squishy. Onion sausages punish high heat twice — once by burning their sugars, once by steaming loose — so medium-low is even more non-negotiable here than in the base recipe.
